candidateRows: Jesus introduced an unusually universal duty to help people in need, and centuries of Christian influence embedded that ethic in the Western moral conscience.
This historical-causal thesis establishes the transformation that both speakers later use to debate whether Western morality is objective or culturally produced.
After the host summarizes the book’s opening claim, Ehrman explains the Western impulse to aid unrelated strangers and traces it from Jesus through Christian control of the Roman world.
Hospitals and similar institutions are good only as a personal judgment, while Jesus historically advanced a distinctive service ethic that reshaped Western institutions and conscience.
The answer explicitly separates historical moral transformation from mind-independent moral goodness, placing the secular account directly against the motion’s realist alternative.
McDowell asks whether Jesus produced an objectively good transformation rather than merely a historical change.

Ehrman calls hospitals, orphanages, and disaster relief good in his personal opinion, denies that this makes the judgment objective, and distinguishes Jesus’s teaching from imperfect Christian practice.
If moral goodness is independent of beliefs and preferences, Ehrman’s description amounts to subjectivism because Jesus’s teachings are not good in themselves on his account.
The move defines the central realist-subjectivist distinction and argues that Ehrman’s historical praise cannot establish objective moral improvement under his stated view.
Ehrman describes charitable institutions as good personally while denying that his personal judgment makes their goodness objective.

McDowell contrasts mind-independent moral facts with preference-dependent judgments, analogizes moral facts to historical and scientific facts, and asks whether subjectivism accurately characterizes Ehrman.
Even if universal objective moral values existed, human beings could access them only through subjective brains and therefore would have no direct access to moral objectivity.
This supplies Ehrman’s principal epistemic objection to claims of objective moral knowledge and redirects the debate from moral examples to the limits of human access.
McDowell asks whether Nazi violence against Jews was universally wrong despite Ehrman’s claim that moral judgments depend on circumstances.
Following a challenge about antisemitism and the Holocaust, Ehrman emphasizes that everyone reasons through a physical human brain and treats this mediation as unavoidable subjectivity.

Different domains use different methods of knowing, so subjective human inquiry does not eliminate objective truth, and immaterial moral truths should not be expected to be accessed like physical facts.
The reply contests the inference from subjective access to absent objective truth and explains why moral knowledge can be objective despite differing from empirical investigation.
Ehrman argues that moral objectivity is inaccessible and that history and science use distinct methods for establishing their respective truth claims.

McDowell accepts that science, history, and morality employ different epistemic means, distinguishes immaterial moral truths from physical matter, and asks how Ehrman knows moral truth is inaccessible.
Human moral inclinations can strongly present actions as right or wrong without implying that any objective moral standard exists beyond those inclinations.
This is the compact core of the secular explanation: morality is grounded in human inclination, while the phenomenology of moral conviction does not establish realism.
McDowell argues that ancient perpetrators violated accessible moral principles and that later societies have made genuine moral progress.
After McDowell claims that child sacrifice and cannibalism were objectively wrong and represent a less developed morality, Ehrman separates powerful human moral responses from external standards.
Ehrman cannot coherently call beliefs superior or describe moral progress if morality consists only of evolved inclinations with no objective standard outside humanity.
The move challenges whether the secular account can preserve normatively meaningful superiority and progress, directly connecting the book’s transformation thesis to moral realism.
Ehrman says moral judgments arise from human inclinations and that such inclinations do not entail an objective standard.
McDowell cites Ehrman’s language about superior beliefs and progress, contrasts it with obligations grounded in human beings bearing God’s image, and compares subjective progress to changing taste.
The priority of helping hungry and homeless strangers is historically recent rather than a universal human moral code, appearing for only a small fraction of Homo sapiens’ existence.
The historical argument uses the late emergence of universal charity to support culturally developed morality and to resist treating present Western values as timelessly universal.
McDowell claims that cultures share transcendent moral principles even when their concrete practices differ.
Ehrman uses aid to hungry and homeless people as a test case, arguing that this priority was absent through most human history and has held high importance for roughly eighteen centuries.
The historical arrival of Jesus’s universal ethic does not make morality subjective, and without objective value Ehrman’s charity is morally indistinguishable from funding racism or sexism.
The move joins both halves of the motion by accepting Jesus’s transformative influence while arguing that meaningful dignity, obligation, and moral distinctions require objective grounding.
Ehrman argues that universal concern for needy strangers is historically recent and therefore should not be claimed as an objective moral value.

McDowell accepts the Christian origin of a universal charitable ethic, grounds human dignity in God’s image, and argues that subjectivism cannot explain why charitable giving is better than harmful causes.

If Jesus transformed Western moral conscience, its difference from earlier human morality undermines McDowell’s claim that his present charitable inclinations straightforwardly express objective truth.
The response turns McDowell’s concession about historical transformation against his realist interpretation by stressing how atypical present Western moral inclinations are across human history.
McDowell argues that historically transformed charitable values remain objectively right and require a distinction unavailable to subjective inclination alone.
Ehrman asks that McDowell’s points be separated, then focuses on their agreement that concern for unrelated needy people was absent through most human history and was transformed by Jesus.
Jesus expanded an already existing cross-cultural moral conscience toward the poor and outsiders, so moral transformation does not contradict enduring objective principles.
This directly reconciles historical moral change with the pro side's claim that objective moral principles existed before Jesus and were broadened through his teaching.
Ehrman's claim that historical transformation of moral conscience undermines McDowell's assertion of accessible objective morality.

After Ehrman argues that transformed moral attitudes imply historically unequal access to alleged objective truth, McDowell distinguishes enduring principles from changing practices and expanded application.
Cross-cultural similarities and differences in moral practice do not establish that morality was given by a superior being or exists objectively.
The move directly rejects the inference from shared moral patterns to divine or objective grounding while preserving the historical thesis about Jesus transforming prior moral traditions.
McDowell's argument that common basic moral principles across cultures support enduring moral objectivity despite Jesus' later expansion.
Ehrman agrees that Jesus transformed something already present but stresses substantial historical variation and denies that shared moral tendencies require divine or objective origins.
The immediate appeal to cross-cultural commonality answers the alleged contradiction, while the deeper issue is which explanation best accounts for shared moral beliefs.
This prevents overstatement of the pro argument and isolates the debate's main inference: whether evolutionary explanation exhausts the evidence or moral belief still points beyond it.
Ehrman's characterization of McDowell as arguing directly from cross-cultural moral similarities to a superior being and objective morality.
Following Ehrman's rejection of a Lewis-style divine inference, McDowell clarifies that commonality first rebuts the inconsistency charge and then raises a comparative explanatory question.
Jesus' major moral innovation was universalizing care beyond kin and social groups so that anyone in need became an appropriate object of help.
This supplies the con side's historical account of Western moral transformation while locating its novelty in expanded scope rather than in revelation of objective moral truths.
Asked what was distinctive about Jesus, Ehrman contrasts evolved in-group altruism and ancient ethical traditions with Jesus' extension of assistance across family, ethnic, and social boundaries.
Calling Jesus' transformation genuine moral progress requires real obligations to aid the poor rather than merely culturally or evolutionarily produced inclinations.
The move directly presses the motion's normative divide by arguing that a historical description of transformed inclinations cannot by itself establish genuine moral improvement or duty.
Ehrman's account of Jesus' universalization of aid as a major moral innovation produced within historical and evolved human development.
McDowell accepts the historical significance of Jesus' worldwide influence but asks whether it was truly better and whether people actually owe aid to strangers and the poor.
Objective grounding is unnecessary because deeply rooted human inclinations and shared human nature provide genuine grounds for belief and moral action.
This states the con side's central metaethical alternative: subjective and evolved human commitments need not be dismissed as merely arbitrary or incapable of guiding conduct.
McDowell's contention that historically or evolutionarily generated inclinations cannot supply actual moral obligations or establish genuine progress.
Ehrman argues that McDowell assumes all meaningful belief and conduct need objective anchors, whereas helping others can be grounded in constitutive human dispositions without external commands.
Contingently evolved feelings cannot explain their own normative authority or why one inclination is morally better than another and therefore binding.
This is the pro side's principal challenge to evolutionary subjectivism: causal origins may explain moral feelings but do not establish reasons, duties, or superiority among competing feelings.
Ehrman's claim that subjectivity grounded in inherent human nature is not a lower basis for truth and can adequately guide moral behavior.
After disputing that he misunderstands evolutionary ethics, McDowell draws on Ehrman's own description of deep commitment arising through natural processes to press the normative-authority gap.
Strong evolved inclinations can coherently guide an entire moral life without proving God or requiring objective values, while historical disagreement challenges claimed objectivity.
The response defends the sufficiency of evolved commitments and turns the historical record into a burden for objective morality rather than evidence requiring divine grounding.
McDowell's argument that feelings produced contingently by evolution lack authority to determine why anyone should be moral or prefer one value over another.
Ehrman uses an ordinary preference analogy to argue that firmly embodied inclinations motivate action without external value, then cites widespread historical divergence as a problem for objectivism.
If morality is only instinct and preference, opposing instincts lack an external standard and condemnations of racism, genocide, sexism, or weaponized religion become inconsistent.
This sharpens the pro side's internal-coherence objection by connecting the absence of an external standard to the con side's own claims of moral superiority and condemnation.
Ehrman's analogy between moral inclination and ordinary drink preferences, together with his claim that evolved subjectivity remains fully coherent.
McDowell grants that instinct explains biological behavior but argues that people possess conflicting impulses, making a standard beyond impulse necessary for moral comparison and criticism.
Subjectivity rooted in inherent human nature can generate moral action and impulses as strong as a realist's, while history and anthropology make objective morality implausible.
This directly answers the coherence challenge and reiterates the con side's central position that motivational strength and moral conduct do not depend on objective grounding.
McDowell's charge that preference-based morality cannot coherently rank opposing instincts or sustain Ehrman's condemnations of harmful conduct and religious behavior.

Ehrman argues that inconsistency appears only if objective value is assumed in advance, then presents moral impulses as humanly rooted and portrays objectivity as psychologically reassuring but historically unsupported.
Human guilt and the perceived need for forgiveness are best explained by a real moral code rather than merely subjective inclination.
The move directly advances the moral-realist explanation of guilt and contrasts objective wrongdoing with historically or scientifically derived knowledge.
After closing several unaddressed topics, McDowell uses Ehrman's discussion of guilt over neglected charity to present an objective-morality explanation and request an alternative.
The human sense of guilt can be explained evolutionarily because dispositions discouraging harm improve community and genetic survival.
This supplies the secular causal explanation specifically requested by McDowell and challenges the claim that guilt requires an objective moral code.
McDowell's claim that guilt reflects actual guilt under a real objective moral code.
In response to the proposed inference from guilt to objective morality, Ehrman attributes guilt to evolved tendencies that reduce harmful behavior within human communities.
People can validly classify actions as right or wrong without an objective standard because moral dispositions are constitutive of human life.
The move directly rejects the asserted need for transcendent grounding while preserving ordinary judgments that some conduct is right and some wrong.
McDowell's contention that right, wrong, guilt, and forgiveness presuppose an objective moral standard.
Ehrman extends his evolutionary answer by maintaining that human moral judgments have adequate grounding in human nature even without a God-given objective standard.
The book's historical account of ethical transformation does not depend on resolving moral objectivity or accepting belief in God.
This limits the claimed implications of the historical thesis and asserts that its account remains applicable to believers and nonbelievers alike.
McDowell's effort to connect the book's moral transformation narrative to the debate over objective and divine grounding.
Ehrman clarifies that his principal thesis concerns historical transformation of ethical sensibilities, while objectivity appears only to explain why morality need not require theism.
A large historical moral transformation raises a further explanatory question about which worldview best accounts for that transformation.
The move reconnects the historical thesis to the motion by distinguishing agreement about the transformation from disagreement about its best explanation.
Ehrman's clarification that his historical transformation argument works independently of belief and moral objectivity.
McDowell accepts that the book makes moral and evolutionary arguments apart from its central historical narrative, but says the scale of transformation still demands explanation.
